method: An open cylindrical pipe carries half a wavelength of its lowest note and a pipe stopped at one end a quarter, so the effective length is the speed of sound divided by twice the frequency for an open pipe and by four times it for a stopped pipe. Air just outside each open end vibrates with the column, so the page subtracts an end correction of 0.6133 times the bore radius at every open end - two for an open pipe, one for the stopped one - to give the length to cut; that is the Levine and Schwinger value for an ideal unflanged tube. The speed of sound is taken as 331.3 m/s times the square root of 1 + theta/273.15 at the air temperature entered, so cold air shortens the pipe and warm air lengthens it. Notes are placed in twelve-tone equal temperament from the reference A4 pitch, and the twelve notes of an equal-tempered octave are listed at the same bore and temperature. A pipe length can be entered instead, and the page then names the nearest note and the offset in cents. The figures describe a straight, smooth, thin-walled cylinder whose open end is cut square: a real instrument's mouth or flue, tone holes, wall thickness, foot, bell, taper and humidity all move the resonance, so the result is a cut length to start from rather than a finished tuning. Inputs are a bore from 2 to 200 mm, air from -20 to 50 degrees Celsius, a reference A4 from 392 to 466 Hz, notes from C1 to C7, and pipe lengths from 20 to 6,000 mm. Nothing is stored, uploaded or fetched; the page runs entirely in the browser.

sources.title: Acoustic resonance - Wikipedia: a cylinder open at both ends resonates at f = n v / 2 L and one closed at an end at f = n v / 4 L for odd n
End correction - Wikipedia: an open end adds about 0.6133 times the radius to the effective length of an ideal cylindrical tube (Levine and Schwinger)
Speed of sound - Wikipedia: dry air at 0 C carries sound at 331.3 m/s, rising with the square root of the absolute temperature
